subject: Meta paid 7.5% to borrow for 30 years
bodyMarkdown:
The AI build out turned into a bond market story this week rather than a stock market one. If you hold a bond fund inside an RRSP or sit in a pension plan, you are quietly on the other side of Meta's data centre spending, and this week the price of that trade went up.

## What Meta paid, and what changed

CNBC reported on Tuesday that Meta went to the market looking for as much as $25 billion in debt to fund its AI spending. It got the money. The part worth your attention is the price. 24/7 Wall St. reported on Wednesday that the 30-year piece of the deal cleared at a yield of about 7.53 per cent, with roughly $58 billion of orders covering the sale 3.87 times. In April, Meta sold 30-year paper at 6.300 per cent. Same company, same AA- rating from S&P, a little over six months apart, and long money now costs it more than a full percentage point extra. The sale came days after S&P moved its outlook on Meta to negative, pointing at the size of the capital spending and at negative free cash flow. Demand did not disappear. It got expensive.

## The debt nobody wants to hold

Underneath the headline deals, the plumbing is backing up. Bloomberg has reported that a bank group led by JPMorgan and MUFG spent more than six months trying to place $38 billion of construction debt for Vantage data centre projects in Texas and Wisconsin leased to Oracle, split into a $23.25 billion facility and a $14.75 billion one, and that some lenders are now willing to sell pieces at a discount. A **project bond**, which is repaid out of one project's own cash flows instead of the parent company's balance sheet, gives the cleanest read on how that risk is being priced. Coverage of the $27.3 billion issue tied to Meta's Hyperion site in Louisiana had it trading near 91 cents on the dollar in October. UBS raised its AI capital spending forecast on Monday to roughly $1 trillion this year and $1.4 trillion in 2027, and said higher volatility is the new normal.

## Why this reaches a Canadian saver

None of these borrowers are Canadian, and that is the point. When the largest borrowers in the world pay up for 30-year money, the long end of the curve reprices everywhere, and Canadian borrowers sit at the same table. The Bank of Canada's own bond yield page had the five-year Government of Canada benchmark at 3.49 per cent on November 3, up from 3.46 the day before. That is the yield five-year fixed mortgages are priced off, and it is the yield Ottawa has to pay on the borrowing plan inside the budget it tables this afternoon. My read is that the AI financing story and our own rate story have become one story. Both come down to what lenders charge for **duration**, the risk of tying up money for decades, at a moment when inflation is above target and governments and hyperscalers are borrowing heavily at the same time.

## The takeaway

If you are shopping a mortgage or a GIC, watch the long end of the yield curve this week rather than the overnight rate. I am tracking two things, whether the next big AI borrower has to pay more than Meta's 7.53 per cent, and whether that Vantage construction loan finally finds buyers. If you hold a broad corporate bond fund, it is worth opening the holdings page and seeing how much of it now sits in technology issuers. Ottawa tables the budget this afternoon, and tomorrow I will take its borrowing plan apart against these same long yields.
